review: Britain's best-selling EV isn't the sharpest thing on this list, and it doesn't need to be. The £41,990 Standard RWD gives up the Premium's air-sprung polish for a 314-mile WLTP figure that translates to a genuine 3.5-3.6 mi/kWh on UK roads, which is why owners stop thinking about range inside a fortnight. The Juniper facelift fixed the worst of the old car's brittleness. Bumps now thud rather than crash, though the firm rear axle still finds every patched B-road, and there's more road roar at 70mph than an Enyaq. A 6.9-second 0-62mph is modest by Tesla standards, but brake feel and steering precision are better than the badge's reputation suggests. What still separates it is logistics: 175kW peak, roughly 27 minutes for 10-80%, and a Supercharger network that removes the planning. Add 854 litres plus a frunk and nothing at this money swallows more. Buy it for the competence, not the theatre.

Strip away the culture war and the Model 3 remains the efficiency benchmark. A 62.5kWh pack returning 332 miles WLTP means roughly 5.3 mi/kWh on paper and a credible 4-plus in the real world, which is how a small battery outruns rivals carrying 20kWh more. At £37,990 for the rear-drive car, 6.2 seconds to 62mph and 175kW charging, the numbers are hard to argue with; the Long Range's 466-mile claim is simply showing off. The Highland revisions cut wind and road noise noticeably, but the ride is still tuned taut rather than plush, and the stalkless, screen-only control layout demands genuine acclimatisation. Rear space is good, the 594-litre boot is deep, yet the saloon aperture makes it far less useful than a hatchback's, and there's no CarPlay. As a company-car proposition with cheap BiK and a working charging network behind it, though, it's still the rational default.

The Q4 e-tron is the most convincing argument in this group for buying comfort over specification. Ride quality on the smaller wheels is genuinely excellent, motorway refinement better still, and the cabin has the density of switchgear and trim that MEB rivals from Skoda and VW can't match. The problem is the arithmetic. £46,250 buys a 59kWh entry car good for 269 miles and 8.1 seconds to 62mph, at which point a Skoda Enyaq 85 with 359 miles undercuts it. Spend up to the 77kWh Performance for 352 miles and 6.6 seconds and it makes far more sense, but you're then past £50,000. Charging is competent rather than quick: 160kW peak, around 28 minutes for 10-80%. The 520-litre boot trails the Enyaq's 585 and there's no frunk. A polished, quiet, easy thing to own, priced as though the badge does more work than it actually does.

This is the fastest-charging car here by a wide margin, and it's the reason to buy one. The 800-volt PPE platform takes 270kW and clears 10-80% in about 21 minutes, so the 100kWh Performance's 398-mile WLTP claim stops being a marketing figure and becomes an actual touring capability. Even the £61,145 83kWh Sport manages 329 miles and better than 3 mi/kWh at motorway pace, which is respectable for a 2.2-tonne SUV. On air suspension it floats along an A-road beautifully; without it, and around town, the mass and the thick pillars make it feel like hard work. Nobody should expect entertainment from the steering. Inside, the screens and the head-up display are properly advanced, though several lower-cabin plastics are beneath the price. 526 litres plus a 64-litre frunk is fine, not generous. A superb long-distance tool, and an expensive way to buy one.

Ford took Volkswagen's MEB hardware and gave it better steering and a far more interesting interior, then undermined the result with the damping. On 20-inch wheels the Explorer is fidgety over broken surfaces and bounces on undulating roads; it settles at motorway speed but never feels as resolved as an Enyaq. Buy it on the smaller rims. The £35,175 Standard RWD's 58kWh pack and 273 miles is the weak end of the range, and 105kW peak charging is slow for 2026 at roughly 30 minutes for 10-80%. The 79kWh Extended Range is the one worth having, with 374 miles and 183kW. Where it earns its keep is inside: the sliding Mega Console, the deep door bins and the sheer quality of the materials are class-leading. Against that, 470 litres is only average, rear legroom is tight for the footprint, and the heat pump remains an option it should not be.

The i4 is the only car in this company that a keen driver would choose on merit. It carries roughly 2.1 tonnes but disguises it with genuinely weighted steering, real front-end bite and body control that stays honest on a fast, bumpy road, and with adaptive dampers it rides better than most rivals as well. Motorway refinement is close to flawless. The £51,950 eDrive35 is quicker than the badge implies at 6.0 seconds, though the eDrive40's 380 miles and 5.6 seconds is the sweeter buy; expect 260-280 real miles from the smaller pack. Charging is the weak point, 180kW peak and about half an hour for 10-80% when an Audi Q6 does it in 21. The 470-litre hatchback boot is usefully shaped, but rear headroom under the sloping roof is poor and depreciation of nearly 40% over three years is real money. Ageing gracefully, not cheaply.

If you want one electric family car to stop thinking about, this is it. The Enyaq rides with a softness that shames cars costing £15,000 more, and at 70mph the cabin is close to silent. The 585-litre boot is the biggest conventional load bay here, the Simply Clever details actually get used, and visibility is excellent. The £39,510 Enyaq 60 is the honest starting point at 268 miles and 8.1 seconds, but the 77kWh Enyaq 85 is the version that makes the case: 359 miles WLTP, 6.7 seconds, and around 240 real miles in British weather. Charging is solid rather than special at 165kW and roughly 24 minutes for 10-80%. What you don't get is any sense of occasion; the steering is inert, the infotainment still stumbles, and options inflate the price quickly. Strong residuals and 4% BiK make the fleet argument close to unanswerable.

The EV3's trick is efficiency. The 81.4kWh Long Range claims 375 miles and returns something close to 4.6 mi/kWh in mild conditions, which puts a £36,000 compact SUV within reach of cars costing twice as much. Even in a British winter it held around 3.3 mi/kWh, and the 58.3kWh entry car at £33,045 still manages 270 miles. Ride quality is soft and forgiving, motorway refinement is good, and 460 litres plus a 25-litre frunk beats the Volvo EX30 comfortably. The compromises are specific rather than fatal. It sits on a 400-volt architecture, so 128kW peak and roughly 31 minutes for 10-80% is well behind an EV6, and the heat pump is reserved for the dearest trim, which is indefensible on a car sold for its efficiency. Cabin plastics are thin in places and the driver-assistance chimes are relentless. Seven-year warranty, strong residuals, few excuses needed.

The Elroq is the Enyaq's argument compressed by 15 centimetres and several thousand pounds, and very little is lost in the process. Rear legroom is still generous, the 470-litre boot only gives away a little to its bigger sibling, and the storage detailing, from the umbrella in the door to the cable net, is the usual Skoda gold standard. From £33,960 with the EV grant applied, the 63kWh SE L 60 does 265 miles and 7.7 seconds; the 82kWh 85 stretches that to 355 miles and 6.4 seconds while charging at 175kW. Either way 10-80% takes around 24-28 minutes, which is competitive at the price. It rides well on the motorway and shrugs off town scruff, though big compressions provoke a float that better-damped rivals resist, the brake pedal is soft and the lower dashboard plastics are cheap. Dull, deliberately, and probably the smartest buy here.

The EX30 sells on design and it deserves to: the recycled-material cabin, the crisp exterior surfacing and the front seats are all genuinely lovely, and around town the soft suspension deals with speed bumps and potholes better than almost anything at the price. It is also absurdly quick. Even the base 51kWh single-motor car does 0-62mph in 5.7 seconds, while the twin-motor P8 manages 3.6, which the chassis has no interest in exploiting. The problems are measurable. 214 miles WLTP from the small battery becomes closer to 160 in cold, fast driving, and testers have seen as little as 68% of the claim; the 69kWh car's 296 miles is the minimum sensible spec. The 318-litre boot is the smallest here by a distance, rear kneeroom is tight, and putting every function including the mirrors behind one central screen is an ergonomic own goal. Style first, and it shows.

The best-looking small car on sale, and one of the very few EVs at this price with a chassis worth talking about. Renault gave the 5 multi-link rear suspension, quick steering and a kerb weight around 1,450kg, and it shows: it corners with real appetite and rewards a committed driver in a way a Kia EV3 never will. Real-world efficiency of about 4 mi/kWh from a car with a standard heat pump is impressive. But the £22,985 entry car's 40kWh pack and 192-mile WLTP claim is thin, 9.0 seconds to 62mph is unhurried, and 80kW charging means around half an hour for 10-80% of a very small battery. The 52kWh Techno at 252 miles and 100kW is the version to buy. Elsewhere the ride is firm and jittery at town speeds, rear legroom is genuinely poor, and 326 litres with a high lip limits it. Character over capability.

Ford has carried the petrol Puma's best qualities across intact. This is one of the few small electric SUVs with real steering feel and an appetite for a twisty road, and the 168bhp front motor makes 8.0 seconds to 62mph feel brisker than the number suggests. The GigaBox under the boot floor survives too, giving 523 litres of genuinely useful, hoseable load space that shames the Volvo EX30's 318. The trade-offs are clear. Ride quality is firm and gets busy on poor surfaces, rear legroom is marginal, and the lower cabin plastics are hard and scratchy. More importantly the 46.8kWh usable pack is small: 259 miles WLTP holds up around town, but sustained motorway running drops efficiency to about 3.2 mi/kWh and the practical range with it. Charging at 100kW and 23 minutes for 10-80% is decent mitigation. A £29,995 city car that can occasionally tour, rather than the reverse.

The Niro EV is a thoroughly sorted car built on obsolete plumbing. Everything about the way it drives is easy to like: a settled, unfussy ride, much-improved sound insulation, light controls, sensible physical switchgear and a 475-litre boot with proper family-car access. 285 miles WLTP from 64.8kWh is honest and around 260 is achievable, while 7.8 seconds to 62mph is adequate. Then you plug it in. Kia rates it at 80kW peak, and 10-80% takes about 43 minutes, which is close to twice what an EV3 needs and roughly double the Audi Q6's 21. On a long journey that difference is the journey. At £37,385 it also now costs more than an EV3 Long Range that goes 90 miles further, charges faster and feels a generation newer, because it is. Excellent as a second-hand purchase; hard to justify at full list.

Nissan built the Ariya as a comfort-first family SUV and largely succeeded. It cruises quietly, the seats genuinely support you on a three-hour run, and the cabin materials embarrass plenty of pricier badges. The catch is that the suspension fidgets over small, sharp inputs around town, which undercuts the calm everywhere else. The 87 kWh car is the one to have: 329 miles claimed, and testers regularly see 260-270 in the real world at around 3.2-3.7 mi/kWh. That is honest rather than impressive. Charging is the weak spot. A 130kW peak means roughly 30 minutes for 10-80%, and the standard 7.4kW AC charger turns an overnight top-up into a 14-hour commitment. The 466-litre boot is adequate but a Skoda Enyaq swallows 585. At £36,990 to start it is priced sensibly against a Model Y or Q4 e-tron, and the interior justifies the ask. Pleasant, well-judged, not class-leading.

range: 240 miles WLTP (52 kWh); 350 miles (79 kWh Pro S)
review: Five years and two facelifts in, the ID.3 has stopped apologising. The cabin finally uses soft-touch materials where your elbows land, the infotainment responds like it should have in 2020, and motorway refinement is genuinely class-competitive. Ride quality splits by wheel size: on 18s it settles nicely, on 20s it thumps around town. Charging is the standout. The 79 kWh Pro S pulls up to 185kW and clears 10-80% in about 26 minutes, which is faster than most of this list and turns a 350-mile claim into a workable long-distance tool. The 59 kWh Pro is the sensible buy, with roughly 213-240 real miles depending on season. The 385-litre boot is squarely shaped and cabin storage is well thought out, though three across the back is a squeeze. Entry pricing at £30,860 is competitive; specify heavily and the maths against an MG4 or Skoda Elroq stops working.

The MG4 remains the value benchmark of the UK EV market, and the 2026 revision fixed most of what was wrong with it. Interior plastics are now soft where it counts, physical climate controls survived, and the 12.8-inch screen is quick. It is rear-driven, sits low, and is measurably more entertaining down a B-road than an ID.3 or Born. The Premium Long Range does 280 miles from 64 kWh and 10-80% in about 25 minutes on a 154kW charger; the 77 kWh Extended Range trades charging speed for 338 miles. Expect around 250 real miles and 3.8 mi/kWh. The compromises are honest: motorway wind and road noise are above average, the ride gets choppy on broken tarmac, and MG's Driver Power reliability standings are poor. But at £29,985 with 388 litres of boot, nothing else here delivers this much car per pound.

The Corsa Electric is the sensible-shoes option, and it wears them well right up until you look at the price list. Efficiency is its real talent: testers see over 4 mi/kWh, which means the 246-mile WLTP figure translates to a genuine 200 miles rather than the usual 20% haircut. Motorway manners are quiet and settled, and the light steering suits town work. Beyond that, the case weakens. The 51 kWh pack peaks at 100kW, so 10-80% takes half an hour, which is mid-pack at best. The 267-litre boot is small even by supermini standards and rear legroom is genuinely poor for adults. Entry pricing of £27,505 looks reasonable; walk up the trim ladder past £32,000 and you are paying MG4 or Renault 5 money for less range, less space and cheaper-feeling switchgear. Buy it on a deal, not on merit.

The second-generation Kona Electric is a quietly excellent piece of packaging. Hyundai grew the car, and the result is 466 litres of boot plus a 27-litre front bin, more rear space than the badge suggests, and doors wide enough to make child-seat wrangling painless. The 65.4 kWh pack is rated at 319 miles on 17-inch wheels, dropping to 282 on 19s, and it holds up well in the real world. Ride quality favours long-travel compliance over body control, so it soaks up urban scars and stays composed at motorway speed, but there is no reward for pushing it on a good road. The disappointment is charging: this is a 400V architecture peaking at around 101kW, so 10-80% takes 34 minutes while an Ioniq 5 does it in 18. Lane-keeping systems that reset every journey grate. At £34,990 with the grant applied, it is still one of the strongest all-rounders here.

Peugeot's E-2008 sells on style and ride, and both are real. It glides over broken surfaces with a fluency that shames far more expensive machinery, and the cabin is one of the better-executed interiors at this money, all knurled metal and interesting textures. The 54 kWh update pushed range to 250 miles, which finally makes it viable rather than apologetic. Everything else is mid-table. The 156hp motor takes 9.1 seconds to 62mph and feels every bit of it, regen is weak even at maximum, and 100kW peak charging means 30 minutes for 10-80%. The 434-litre boot is usefully square with no load lip, but rear legroom and headroom are tight, and i-Cockpit still forces you to choose between seeing the dials and holding the wheel properly. The problem is £36,500, which puts it alongside a Kona Electric with more power, more range and more space. Handsome, comfortable, and hard to justify.

The iX1 is the most convincingly premium object in this group. Material quality, switchgear feel and BMW's Operating System 9 are all a class above, and 490 litres of boot with 1,495 seats-down makes it the practicality winner here despite compact dimensions. Efficiency is strong too, 3.6-4.3 mi/kWh, which turns the eDrive20's 318-mile claim into something like 270 real miles. Then you drive it over a British B-road. The suspension is tuned tight and the extra 300kg of battery gives it a jiggly, occasionally brittle secondary ride that the Skoda Elroq simply does not have. The 130kW charge ceiling is dated: 29 minutes for 10-80% when a Model Y manages the same in 15. The xDrive30 is genuinely quick at 5.6 seconds, but it costs £43,005 and drops range to 288 miles. From £37,065 you are paying a badge premium for a car that is out-ranged and out-ridden by cheaper rivals.

range: 265 miles WLTP (59 kWh); 389 miles (79 kWh VZ)
review: The Born is an ID.3 wearing a leather jacket, and that is less damning than it sounds. Cupra firmed the springs, sharpened the steering and fitted properly bolstered bucket seats, and the result rides better than the hardware suggests while still cruising with real composure. Efficiency is a genuine strength: over 4 mi/kWh in normal use, more if you are gentle, so the 59 kWh entry car's 265-mile claim mostly stands up. Rapid charging is among the best here at roughly 26 minutes for 10-80%. What it isn't is fun. The VZ's 326hp and 5.6-second sprint deliver speed rather than involvement, the brakes feel spongy, and there is no true one-pedal mode. The infotainment still crashes, climate control is touchscreen-only, and Cupra sat 28th of 31 brands for owner satisfaction. From £35,690 with 385 litres of boot and a five-year warranty, it is a good family EV pretending to be a hot hatch.

The Dolphin's pitch is space and kit for the money, and on rear legroom it genuinely delivers, with room behind a six-footer that shames cars a class above. Standard equipment is comprehensive, the six-year warranty is reassuring, and BYD's Blade LFP chemistry should age well. But the details let it down. The suspension is soft on smooth roads and crashes over sharp-edged potholes, motorway noise is intrusive, and the rotating touchscreen looks clever while burying climate controls two menus deep. Charging is the real problem: an 88kW ceiling means roughly 41 minutes for 10-80%, slow enough to matter on any journey over 200 miles. Real-world range lands near 240 miles at 4.0 mi/kWh, which is respectable. The 364-litre boot has a high load lip and there is no frunk. At £30,220 it sits awkwardly between an MG4 that drives better and goes further, and a Renault 5 that is simply more charming.

This is the one car here bought with the heart, and it makes no apology for it. The Cooper Electric steers with the immediacy Mini has always promised, turns in flat and eager, and the Oxford-built cabin, with its circular OLED display and knitted textiles, is the most characterful interior in the group by a wide margin. It is also deeply compromised. The ride is firm to the point of bouncy on anything other than good tarmac. The 200-litre boot is the smallest on this list by 67 litres, and rear seats are a formality. The Cooper E's 41 kWh pack manages 190 miles WLTP and closer to 150 in winter, with a 75kW charge ceiling; the SE's 54.2 kWh and 249 miles is the version worth having, but it starts at £34,905. From £26,905 the E is fairly priced for what it is. Just be honest about what that is: a brilliant second car.

The 2022 rear-drive rework transformed the Polestar 2 from a curiosity into a properly engineered car. The Long Range Single Motor claims 406 miles and testers comfortably clear 300 in mixed use, which is the best range-to-reality ratio on this list. It charges at up to 205kW, so 10-80% takes about 28 minutes, and the Google-native infotainment remains the benchmark for how in-car software should work. Chassis tuning is unambiguously firm. On a good road it is precise, flat and genuinely rewarding; at 20mph over cracked city tarmac it is unforgiving, and no amount of Scandinavian minimalism disguises that. The 407-litre boot plus 41-litre frunk is decent but not saloon-class, and the low roofline costs rear headroom, especially with the panoramic glass. At £45,210 it undercuts a BMW i4 and out-builds a Model 3. Buy it for the range and the quality, not for a soft ride.

Geely engineered the #1 and Mercedes styled it, and the combination produces the most comfortable small EV here. The suspension is deliberately soft, so it lollops over speed humps and expansion joints in a way nothing else in this price bracket manages, and motorway noise levels are low. The cabin is genuinely lovely, with an excellent, fast infotainment system and more rear headroom than the compact footprint suggests. Every version gets 268hp and a 6.7-second sprint, which is more pace than the chassis wants; lean on it through a corner and it rolls and gives up. Charging is a strong point at up to 150kW and roughly 30 minutes for 10-80%. Range is the weakness. The £29,950 49 kWh car claims 193 miles and returns closer to 170; the 66 kWh Premium at 273 miles is the one to buy. A 313-litre boot and 15-litre frunk seal its status as a comfortable urban car, not a tourer.
